text:
The U.S. Commerce and Justice Departments have released a detailed timeline of their Megaspeed investigation, confirming $NVDA stopped selling to the Singapore data-center company in June 2025, when it was placed on Nvidia's internal "no sell" list.

Here's what the joint statement reveals:

2024: Commerce opened an investigation after detecting suspicious activity suggesting possible diversion of sensitive U.S. semiconductors.

May 2025: Investigators requested Nvidia's records covering direct and indirect sales to Megaspeed.

June 2025: Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its internal "no sell" list.

June 2025: U.S. and Singaporean authorities conducted an on-site inspection of Megaspeed and interviewed its then-CEO, Alice Huang.

Afterward: The Justice Department took the lead in the criminal investigation.

The disclosure comes after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent criticized Commerce for not placing Megaspeed on the U.S. trade blacklist, despite support from four federal agencies.

Importantly, Nvidia's internal "no sell" list is separate from the government's Entity List.

Source: U.S. Commerce and Justice Departments

• Up 14.7% from September

October already beat the top of that analyst range. If the next two months simply match October, Q4 lands near the top of guidance.

The drivers are AI demand and 2nm shipments, now TSMC's most advanced process in commercial production.

TSMC raised its 2026 growth forecast to ~44% in October. With the biggest quarter still in progress, that looks safe.

Customers were already looking to diversify compute, improve economics and reduce dependence on NVIDIA. Leadership uncertainty gives them another reason to evaluate alternatives.

Existing GPU clusters won’t suddenly get replaced. The competition is for new training runs, inference workloads and multiyear capacity commitments.

NVIDIA is also very expensive — only really worth it for training, not for inference. 

I think $GOOGL is very much worth a long here.

name: Serenity
zh_summary: @aleabitoreddit discusses laser players for CPO: Lightmatter CEO notes 8 optical engines/GPU is 100x more lasers. Mentions $AVGO projections, $LITE and $COHR most de-risked with long-term visibility. AI trade moves together.
en_summary: @aleabitoreddit discusses laser players for CPO: Lightmatter CEO notes 8 optical engines/GPU is 100x more lasers. Mentions $AVGO projections, $LITE and $COHR most de-risked with long-term visibility. AI trade moves together.
text:
Just in general for laser players, from Lightmatter's CEO, regarding scale up CPO:

8 optical engines/GPU introduces 100x more lasers than scale out switching. More conservative estimates were 10x laser content from AOI's CFO. 

Along with ASPs for those lasers going higher (eg. 10x ASPs than pluggables for single emitter UHP lasers).

From what I've seen yearly capacity expansion for lasers generally increase around ~3x Y/Y like $AVGO projections, or ~5x over 2-3 years like Furukawa's. 

This is what I mean by optical content like lasers + requirements (more InP substrates), rises per generation and bottlenecks on UHP ranges might persist through 2030 despite aggregate capex decreasing.

Which is what I'm trying to argue here. 

Future CPO laser competitors like Furukawa/AOI/Shija are more nuanced, since AOI is focused on 800G/1.6T transceivers (which faced capacity expansion delays + DSP Bottlenecks), but they have capability for 400mW+ ranges + ongoing CPO qualifications. 

I don't think transceivers have the same durability though in capex reduction scenarios, which is why I've been arguing the valuable optionality AOI has to focus on merchant lasers is mispriced. 

A lot of it is execution/qualification rather than demand, $LITE + $COHR are the most de-risked with confirmed long term visibility. 

But entire AI trade is moving up and down together.

BofA Securities kept its Buy rating on $TSM with a price objective of $620 per share, 55% above the $398 price at publication. 

The note focuses on Arizona: a new long-term power contract that lifts the site's electricity supply to 1.88 GW, enough in BofA's estimate to triple advanced-node capacity, and evidence that the US fabs are profitable even before government grants.

The numbers behind BofA's estimate:

- Power: TSMC and Arizona Public Service signed a long-term agreement that extends electricity service to 1.88 GW at full buildout, up from 1.2 GW. Because TSMC makes an upfront credit-support payment in January 2027, APS treats the full 1.88 GW as committed demand and could supply more. 

- Capacity: At about 10 MW per 1,000 wafers a month of advanced-node capacity, plus some power for back-end packaging, BofA estimates the site could reach ~150k wafers a month, against ~50k by Q4 2027. That is roughly three times the 2027 level. 

- Revenue: At the current build cadence this could be in place by 2035, before the additional facilities announced earlier this year, and generate more than $60bn of revenue a year. For scale, BofA expects TSMC's total revenue to be about $176bn in 2026. 

Securing power years ahead is what turns announced fabs into a buildable plan. The deal removes one of the main physical constraints on the US expansion and gives customers seeking US-made chips more visibility on supply.

$MSFT - MICROSOFT REVEALS MONTHS-OLD BUG BEHIND GLOBAL OUTAGE

Microsoft says a software bug undetected since July triggered last week's worldwide disruption affecting Outlook, Teams, Copilot and other services.

The failure began on November 11, when routine traffic rerouting overloaded servers and caused cascading system failures.

At the outage's peak, more than 80% of Outlook servers were unresponsive.

Microsoft took approximately 30 hours to identify the broader problem and begin deploying a fix.

The incident raises fresh concerns over cloud infrastructure resilience and enterprise dependence on Microsoft.

text:
🚨 JOURNEE DE PURGE SUR LA TECH

Je pense qu'on sous estime ce qui est entrain de se jouer actuellement au regarde de Nvidia et l'IPO d'Anthropic

Ce qu'il faut retenir

Après un Taiex à -6,03 % cette nuit, sa deuxième plus grosse baisse en points de l'histoire, Wall Street traîne sur les plus bas de séance. Vers 19h15 (Paris), le $SOXX perd 4,7 %, le Nasdaq 100 -2,3 % et le S&P 500 -1,6 %. Le VIX prend 14 % vers 22 et le 10 ans US reste collé à 5,13 %

1. Washington serre la vis en Asie du Sud-Est

Le Commerce impose désormais une licence pour exporter des puces IA avancées en Indonésie, Malaisie, Singapour, Thaïlande et au Brésil, sauf pour les clients à maison mère américaine, et une autre pour louer du calcul en volume à une société chinoise depuis un datacenter étranger. La Street doute que la règle morde vraiment, entre sociétés écrans et usages déclarés autrement, et pense qu'elle touchera surtout les petits néoclouds plutôt que les hyperscalers

Vers 19h15, $MU -7 %, $MRVL -6,3 %, $TSM -5,4 %, $AMD -5,2 %, $CRWV -7 % et $NBIS -7,3 %. La Street vend ses gagnants pour financer ses ordres sur Anthropic. Beaucoup jugent la baisse de TSMC exagérée, la capacité libérée serait vite reprise par Google, AMD et Broadcom

2. Nvidia, la journée des contradictions

Le matin, Trump ouvre la porte. Interrogé sur un retour de Jensen comme CEO, il répond « ça ne me dérangerait certainement pas » et ajoute « je pense qu'il a appris une grosse leçon ». Selon les dépêches, il juge aussi q
